modules.name: Force and Newton's Laws of Motion

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Force:

Any push or pull which either changes or tends to change the state of rest or of uniform motion (constant velocity) of a body is known as force.

Effects of Force: A non-zero resultant force may produce the following effects on a body.

(1) It may change the speed of the body.

(2) It may change the direction of motion.

(3) It may change both the speed and direction of motion.

(4) It may change the size and the shape of the body.

Units for measurement of force: -

Absolute units:

(1) S.I :- Newton (N)

(2) C.G.S :- Dyne

Conversion:

$1 \mathrm{~N}=10^5$Dyne

Force is a vector quantity, with magnitude and direction.

Newton’s First law of motion: If a body is at rest, then it remains at rest and if it is moving with constant velocity then it continues to move with constant velocity until or unless it is acted upon by an external force.

Inertia: It is the property of a body by virtue of which it opposes any change in its state of rest or state of motion.

Mass of a body is quantitative or numerical measure of a body's inertia.

Inertia $\propto$ Mass

1.Inertia of Rest : It is the inability of a body to change its state of rest by itself.

2.Inertia of Motion :It is the inability of a body to change its state of uniform motion by itself.

3.Inertia of Direction: It is the inability of a body to change its direction of motion by itself.

Newton’s Second Law of Motion: According to this law, "rate of change of momentum of any system is directly proportional to the applied external force."

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}_{\mathrm{net}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}}{\mathrm{dt}}$

For variable mass system e.g. conveyor belt, rocket net Force is represented as

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}_{\mathrm{net}}=\frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} \mathrm{dm}}{\mathrm{dt}}$

The slope of momentum-time graph is equal to the force on the particle at that instant.

$\mathrm{F}=\frac{\mathrm{dp}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\tan \theta=\text { slope }$

Newton Third Law of Motion: According to Newton's third law, to every action, there is always an equal (in magnitude) and opposite (in direction) reaction. This law is also known as action-reaction law.

Here, (force on first body due to second body) is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to (force on second body due to first body).

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}_{12}=-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}_{21}$

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.question: A cricket ball of mass 150 g is moving with a velocity of 12 m/s and is hit by a bat so that the ball gets turned back with a velocity of 20 m/s. If the duration of contact between the ball and bat is 0.01 s, find the change in momentum and magnitude of required force?
blocks.answer:
According to given problem change in momentum of the ball

$\Delta \mathrm{\vec p}=\mathrm{\vec p}_{\mathrm{f}}-\mathrm{\vec p}_{\mathrm{i}}=\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{ \vec v}-\mathrm{\vec u})=150 \times 10^{-3}[20-(-12)]=4.8 \mathrm{~N}\mathrm{s}$

$\left|\vec{F}_{\text {avg }}\right|$= $\dfrac{\Delta \mathrm{p}}{\Delta \mathrm{t}}=\dfrac{4.80}{0.01}=480 \mathrm{~N}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Impulse: When a large force is applied on a body for a very short interval of time, then the product of force and time interval is known as impulse.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{d} \mathrm{I}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}} \mathrm{dt}=\mathrm{d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}} \quad\left[\because \frac{\mathrm{~d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}\right]$

Unit of impulse = N·s or kg·m/s.

Dimension of impulse: [M1L1T–1]

Case-1 : If this force is acting from time t1 to t2

$\begin{aligned} & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{I}}=\int_{\mathrm{t}_1}^{t_2} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~F}} \mathrm{dt}=\int_{\bar{p}_1}^{\bar{p}_2} \mathrm{~d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}} \\ & \text { Impulse }=\text { Change in momentum } \end{aligned}$

Case-2 : If constant or average force acts on a body

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{I}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}_{\text {avg }} \Delta \mathrm{t}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}_2-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{P}}_1$

Case3 : Impulse from force time graph : Area under the force time graph represents impulse or change in momentum.

$\mathrm{\vec I}=\Delta \mathrm{\vec p}=\int \mathrm{\vec Fdt}=$ Net area under F-t  graph

Average Force: Average force acting on a body in a given time interval can be calculated by

$\displaystyle {\vec F_{avg}} = \frac{{\Delta \vec p}}{{\Delta t}}$

Note: For a certain momentum change if the time interval is increased, then the average force exerted on body will decrease.

Impulse Momentum Theorem: Impulse-momentum theorem states that the impulse applied to an object will be equal to the change in its momentum.

$\text { Impulse }=\mathrm{\vec F} \times \Delta \mathrm{t}=\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{\vec v}-\mathrm{\vec u})$

Linear Momentum

The total amount of motion possessed by a moving body is known as the momentum of the body.

• It is the product of the mass and velocity of a body.
    • It is a vector quantity whose direction is along instantaneous velocity.
    • Momentum    $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}=\mathrm{m} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}}$    ( Momentum = Mass × Velocity)
    • SI Unit-kg-m/s, N-s  Dimension : [MLT–1]

Conservation of Linear Momentum:

According to Newton’s Second law, if net external force on the system is zero, then linear momentum of the system remains conserved.

$\text { If } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}_{\mathrm{ext}}=\overrightarrow{0} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{~d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\overrightarrow{0} \Rightarrow \overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}=\text { constant } \Rightarrow \overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}_{\mathrm{in}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{p}}_{\mathrm{final}}$

Examples of Law of Conservation of Momentum

1. Air-filled balloons

2. System of gun and bullet

3. Motion of rockets

Variable Mass Problems(Rocket Propulsion):

Case-1 : If rocket is accelerating upwards, then -

Net upwards force on rocket = ma

$v_{\text{rel}} \left| \frac{dm}{dt} \right| - mg = ma  $

$\text{Where } v_{\text{rel}} \text{ is the relative velocity of the ejected mass w.r.t rocket}$

Case-2 : If rocket is moving with constant velocity, then a = 0

$\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{rel}}\left|\frac{\mathrm{dm}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right|=\mathrm{mg}$

modules.name: Common Forces in Mechanics and FBD

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
1.Weight : Weight is the gravitational force with which the earth pulls an object. The weight of an object is mg, where g is acceleration due to gravity.

2.Tension : A pulling force exerted on an object by a rope or string. This is a contact force.

3.Normal Reaction : The contact force by which two surfaces in contact push each other perpendicular to the contacting surfaces, is known as normal reaction.

4.Spring force: It is the force exerted by a spring when it is compressed or stretched from its equilibrium position. It follows Hooke's Law, which states that the force is proportional to the displacement of the spring.

5.Friction : It is a force that is set up between the surfaces of contact, when one body slides or tends to do so on the surface of another body.

Free Body Diagram: A diagram showing all external forces acting on an object is called "Free Body Diagram" (F.B.D.)

Problems on Normal Reaction

$\mathrm{a}=\dfrac{\mathrm{F}_{\text {net }}}{\mathrm{m}_{\text {total }}}$

$\mathrm{a}=\dfrac{\mathrm{F}}{\mathrm{~m}_1+\mathrm{m}_2}$

$\mathrm{N}=\dfrac{\mathrm{m}_2 \mathrm{~F}}{\mathrm{~m}_1+\mathrm{m}_2} \text { (here } \mathrm{N}=\text { contact force) }$

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
A block of mass M is pulled along a horizontal frictionless surface by a rope of mass m as shown in fig. A horizontal force F is applied to one end of the rope. Find the

(i) Acceleration of the rope and the block

(ii) Force that the rope exerts on the block.

(iii) Tension in the rope at its mid-point.
blocks.answer:
(i) Acceleration $\mathrm{a}=\frac{\mathrm{F}}{(\mathrm{m}+\mathrm{M})}$

(ii) Force exerted by the rope on the block is

$\mathrm{T}=\mathrm{Ma}=\frac{\mathrm{M} \cdot \mathrm{~F}}{(\mathrm{~m}+\mathrm{M})}$

(iii) $\quad \mathrm{T}_1=\left(\frac{\mathrm{m}}{2}+\mathrm{M}\right) \mathrm{a}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{m}+2 \mathrm{M}}{2}\right)\left(\frac{\mathrm{F}}{\mathrm{m}+\mathrm{M}}\right)$

Tension in rope at midpoint is  $\mathrm{T}_1=\frac{(\mathrm{m}+2 \mathrm{M}) \mathrm{F}}{2(\mathrm{~m}+\mathrm{M})}$
blocks.prompt:
A block of mass M is pulled along a horizontal frictionless surface by a rope of mass m as shown in fig. A horizontal force F is applied to one end of the rope. Find the

(i) Acceleration of the rope and the block

(ii) Force that the rope exerts on the block.

(iii) Tension in the rope at its mid-point.

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: Two blocks of masses m = 2 kg and M = 5 kg are in contact on a frictionless table. A horizontal force F (= 35 N) is applied to m. Find the force of contact between the blocks. Will the force of contact remain same if F is applied to M?
blocks.answer:
As the blocks are rigid both will move with same acceleration under the action of a force F

$\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{a}=\frac{\mathrm{F}}{\mathrm{~m}+\mathrm{M}}=\frac{35}{2+5}=5 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\\ &\text { Force of contact } \mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{M}}=\mathrm{Ma}=5 \times 5=25 \mathrm{~N} \end{aligned}$

If the force is applied to M then its action on m will be

$\mathrm{N}_{\mathrm{m}}=\mathrm{ma}=2 \times 5=10 \mathrm{~N}$

From this problem it is clear that magnitude of acceleration does not depend on the fact that whether the force is applied to m or M, but force of contact does.
blocks.prompt: Two blocks of masses m = 2 kg and M = 5 kg are in contact on a frictionless table. A horizontal force F (= 35 N) is applied to m. Find the force of contact between the blocks. Will the force of contact remain same if F is applied to M?

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
• Ignoring Directions: Force and momentum are vectors; consider their direction.
  • Confusing Mass and Weight: Mass is constant; weight depends on gravitational force.
  • Forgetting Units: Always ensure unit consistency.
  • By mistake making FBD of other body.
  • By mistake showing incorrect action-reaction pairs of normal (N) or tension (T)

modules.name: Frame of Reference & Pseudo Force & Weighing Machine

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Frame of Reference: A system with respect to which position or motion of a particle is described is known as frame of reference.

1. Inertial Frame of Reference :The frame for which law of inertia is applicable is known as inertial frame of reference.

All the frames which are at rest or moving uniformly with respect to an inertial frame, are also inertial frame.

2. Non-inertial frame of Reference: The frame for which law of inertia is not applicable is known as non-inertial frame of reference.

All the frames which are accelerating or rotating with respect to an inertial frame will be non-inertial frames.

Pseudo Force: To apply Newton’s law of motion in non-inertial reference frame we need to apply pseudo force. It is an imaginary force which is used to explain the motion of objects from non-inertial reference frames.

Magnitude :

$\mathrm{F}_{\text {pesudo }}$=Mass of body $\times$ Acceleration of non-inertial frame (Observer)

Direction : Opposite to the direction of acceleration of non-inertial frame(observer)

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}_{\mathrm{pseudo}}=-\mathrm{m} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\mathrm{obs}}$

Note: Pseudo force does not follow action reaction law.

Weighing machine

It measures the Normal Reaction applied on it

Reading of weighing machine is also called Apparent weight.

$\mathrm{W}_{\text {app }}=\text { Normal Reaction on machine }$

$\text { Reading }(\mathrm{kg}-\mathrm{wt})=\dfrac{\text { Normal Reaction }(\mathrm{in~N})}{\mathrm{g}}$

Effective or Apparent weight of a man in lift

Case-1 : If the lift is at rest or moving uniformly (a = 0), then

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{app}}=\mathrm{N} \\ & \mathrm{~W}_{\mathrm{actual}}=\mathrm{mg} \end{aligned}$

Case-2 : If the lift is accelerated upwards, then

$\mathrm{N}=\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{~g}+\mathrm{a})$

$\mathrm{W}_{\text {app }}>\mathrm{W}_{\text {actual }}$

Case-3 : If the lift is accelerated downwards, then

$\mathrm{N}=\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{~g}-\mathrm{a})$

$\mathrm{W}_{\text {app }}<\mathrm{W}_{\text {actual }}$

Case-4: If the lift is under free fall, it implies that its acceleration is equal to the acceleration due to gravity. i.e. a = g, then

$W_{\text {app }}=0$

It means that person in lift will feel weightless. The apparent weight of any body falling freely is zero

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: A pendulum of mass m is suspended from the ceiling of a train moving with constant acceleration 'a' as shown in figure. Find the angle $\theta$ in which pendulum is in equilibrium w.r.t. train. Also calculate tension in the string.
blocks.answer:
With respect to train, the bob is in equilibrium

$\therefore \quad \Sigma \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{y}}=0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{~T} \cos \theta=\mathrm{mg}..........(i)$

and

$\quad \Sigma \mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{x}}=0 \Rightarrow \mathrm{~T} \sin \theta=\mathrm{ma}...........(ii)$

Dividing equation (ii) by (i)

$\tan \theta=\frac{\mathrm{a}}{\mathrm{g}} \Rightarrow \theta=\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{\mathrm{a}}{\mathrm{g}}\right)$

Squaring and adding equation

$\mathrm{T}=\mathrm{m} \sqrt{\mathrm{a}^2+\mathrm{g}^2}$

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: What horizontal acceleration should be provided to the wedge so that the block of mass m kept on wedge remains at rest w.r.t. wedge?
blocks.answer:
For equilibrium along wedge

(In reference of wedge frame)

$\displaystyle \begin{array}{ll} \operatorname{macos} \theta & =m g \sin \theta \\ \Rightarrow & a=g \frac{\sin \theta}{\cos \theta} \\ \Rightarrow & a=g \tan \theta \end{array}$

blocks.text:

  • By mistake forgetting application of pseudo force in non inertial frame.
  • By mistake taking incorrect direction of pseudo force.

modules.name: Friction(Contact Force, Angle of Friction & Angle of Repose)

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Friction: Friction is a force that is set up between the surfaces of contact, when one body slides or tends to do so on the surface of another body. It opposes relative motion between two bodies.

Cause of Friction: Friction arises on account of Intermolecular forces of attraction between the two surfaces at the point of actual contact.

Friction depends on the following factors:

1.Friction force depends only on the area covered by contact particles of contact surfaces (actual contact area) it does not depend on the area covered by the body (apparent contact area)

2. Except static friction (fs), friction force depends on normal reaction (N) f $\propto$ N

Types of Friction

1. Static Friction: When two bodies have tendency to move over each other (but they are not moving w.r.t. to each other) then the force opposing tendency of motion is known as static friction.

Maximum value of static friction is called limiting friction

$f_s \leq f_L
$

2. Limiting Friction: The maximum value of static friction is known as limiting friction.

$\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{L}} \propto \mathrm{~N} \Rightarrow \mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{L}}=\mu_{\mathrm{S}} \mathrm{~N}$

µs : Coefficient of static friction

3.Kinetic Friction: When two contact surfaces slide on each other, friction acting between them is called Kinetic/Dynamic friction.

$\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{k}}=\mu_{\mathrm{k}} \mathrm{~N}$

µk = coefficient of kinetic friction.

Graph between applied force and force of friction:

Contact Force:

$\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{C}}=\sqrt{\mathrm{f}^2+\mathrm{N}^2}$

2.Angle of Friction ($\lambda$):The  angle which the resultant of the force of limiting friction fL and normal reaction N makes with the direction of normal reaction N.

$\tan \lambda=\mu_{\mathrm{s}}$

Angle of Repose :It is defined as the minimum angle of inclination of a plane with the horizontal at which a body placed on it just begins to slide down or equivalently the maximum angle of inclination of plane with the horizontal at which a body placed on it does not slide.

$\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{L}}=\mathrm{mg} \sin \theta ........(i)$

$\mathrm{~N}=\mathrm{mg} \cos \theta \\$

$\mathrm{~f}_{\mathrm{L}}=\mu \mathrm{N}=\mu \mathrm{mg} \cos \theta ........(ii)$

From (i) and (ii)

$\mu_s=\dfrac{\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{L}}}{\mathrm{~N}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{mg} \sin \theta}{\mathrm{mg} \cos \theta}=\tan \theta \Rightarrow \theta=\tan ^{-1} \mu_s$

$\text { Angle of repose }(\theta)=\text { Angle of friction }(\lambda)$

Downward sliding on rough incline plane: If angle of inclination is greater than the angle of repose, then the body accelerates down the incline.

$\mathrm{a}=\mathrm{g}\left[\sin \theta-\mu_{\mathrm{k}} \cos \theta\right] \quad \text { hence } \mathrm{a}<\mathrm{g}$

For sliding down with constant velocity: a = 0

$\mathrm{g} \sin \theta=\mu_{\mathrm{k}} \mathrm{~g} \cos \theta$

$\tan \theta=\mu_{\mathrm{k}}$

Upward sliding on rough incline:

$a=g \sin \theta+\mu_k g \cos \theta$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Consider two blocks A and B placed one above the other, resting on a horizontal surface. A horizontal force F applied on either blocks, tend to move the system of blocks. Problems involving such situations can conveniently be solved by following mentioned steps:

Step 1 : Draw the FBD of the combined block system. If friction appears in the FBD, then take its limiting value (maximum static friction).

If applied force > limiting friction then motion is possible, otherwise not.

If movement occurs then, either the blocks move together or separately depending on the fact that whether frictional forces are able to support the combined motion or not.

Step 2: Assuming combined motion, find the common acceleration $a_c$. Draw the FBD of the body on which external force is not applied. Find the frictional force f required to make it move combinedly with the other block. Compare the above-calculated force with the limiting value $\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{L}}$ (maximum static friction).

If $ \mathrm{f} \leq \mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{L}}$, then both move together with common acceleration $ \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{c}}$. Otherwise, they move separately.

Step 3 : For separate motion, draw the individual FBD's of both blocks with kinetic friction forces acting wherever applicable. Find the individual accelerations of the two blocks using Newton's second law.

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question: Calculate the accelerations of the blocks and the force of friction between them.
blocks.answer:
Step 1 : Draw FBD of the combined block system.

Obviously, there is an unbalanced force F=50N in the horizontal direction.

$\therefore $ Movement occurs.

Step 2 : Assuming that the blocks move together with common acceleration.

$\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{50}{5+10}=3.33 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$

draw the FBD of block B (on which external force is not applied)

Required frictional force

$\mathrm{f}=\mathrm{m}_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{c}}=10 \times 3.33=33.3 \mathrm{~N}$

$f_2=20 \mathrm{~N}$

Obviously, f exceeds $\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{L}} $.

$\therefore$ The two blocks move separately.

Step 3 : Draw the individual FBD's of the two blocks

Applying Newton's II law, in the horizontal direction.

$\mathrm{a}_1=\frac{50-20}{5}=6 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$ and

$\mathrm{a}_2=\frac{20}{10}=2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$

Force of friction between the blocks $20 \mathrm{~N}$.
blocks.prompt: Calculate the accelerations of the blocks and the force of friction between them.

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: Blocks A and B of masses 5 kg and 10 kg are placed as shown in figure. If block A is pulled with 50 N . Find out the acceleration of A and B. If coefficient of friction between A and B is 0.5 and between B and ground is 0.4.
blocks.answer:
Solution:

FBDs of blocks:

Limiting friction between A and B,

$f_{1 L}=\mu_1 N_1=0.5 \times 5 g=24.5 \mathrm{~N}$

Limiting friction between B and ground,

$f_{2 L}=\mu_2 \mathrm{~N}_2=0.4 \times 15 \mathrm{~g}=58.8 \mathrm{~N}$

For Block A,

$50-\mathrm{f}_1=5 \times \mathrm{a}$

$\Rightarrow 50-24.5=5 \times \mathrm{a}$

$\Rightarrow \mathrm{a}=5.1 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2$

Block B will remain at rest, become {f_{1L}} < {f_{2L}}$.

All the frames which are accelerating or rotating with respect to an inertial frame will be non-inertial frames.

Pseudo Force: To apply Newton’s law of motion in non-inertial reference frame we need to apply pseudo force. It is an imaginary force which is used to explain the motion of objects from non-inertial reference frames.

Magnitude :

$\mathrm{F}_{\text {pesudo }}$=Mass of body $\times$ Acceleration of non-inertial frame (Observer)

Direction : Opposite to the direction of acceleration of non-inertial frame(observer)

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}_{\mathrm{pseudo}}=-\mathrm{m} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{a}}_{\mathrm{obs}}$

Note: Pseudo force does not follow action reaction law.

Weighing machine

It measures the Normal Reaction applied on it

Reading of weighing machine is also called Apparent weight.

$\mathrm{W}_{\text {app }}=\text { Normal Reaction on machine }$

$\text { Reading }(\mathrm{kg}-\mathrm{wt})=\dfrac{\text { Normal Reaction }(\mathrm{in~N})}{\mathrm{g}}$

Effective or Apparent weight of a man in lift

Case-1 : If the lift is at rest or moving uniformly (a = 0), then

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{app}}=\mathrm{N} \\ & \mathrm{~W}_{\mathrm{actual}}=\mathrm{mg} \end{aligned}$

Case-2 : If the lift is accelerated upwards, then

$\mathrm{N}=\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{~g}+\mathrm{a})$

$\mathrm{W}_{\text {app }}>\mathrm{W}_{\text {actual }}$

Case-3 : If the lift is accelerated downwards, then

$\mathrm{N}=\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{~g}-\mathrm{a})$

$\mathrm{W}_{\text {app }}<\mathrm{W}_{\text {actual }}$

Case-4: If the lift is under free fall, it implies that its acceleration is equal to the acceleration due to gravity. i.e. a = g, then

$W_{\text {app }}=0$

It means that person in lift will feel weightless. The apparent weight of any body falling freely is zero

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Friction: Friction is a force that is set up between the surfaces of contact, when one body slides or tends to do so on the surface of another body. It opposes relative motion between two bodies.

Cause of Friction: Friction arises on account of Intermolecular forces of attraction between the two surfaces at the point of actual contact.

Friction depends on the following factors:

1.Friction force depends only on the area covered by contact particles of contact surfaces (actual contact area) it does not depend on the area covered by the body (apparent contact area)

2. Except static friction (fs), friction force depends on normal reaction (N) f $\propto$ N

Types of Friction

1. Static Friction: When two bodies have tendency to move over each other (but they are not moving w.r.t. to each other) then the force opposing tendency of motion is known as static friction.

Maximum value of static friction is called limiting friction

$f_s \leq f_L
$

2. Limiting Friction: The maximum value of static friction is known as limiting friction.

$\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{L}} \propto \mathrm{~N} \Rightarrow \mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{L}}=\mu_{\mathrm{S}} \mathrm{~N}$

µs : Coefficient of static friction

3.Kinetic Friction: When two contact surfaces slide on each other, friction acting between them is called Kinetic/Dynamic friction.

$\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{k}}=\mu_{\mathrm{k}} \mathrm{~N}$

µk = coefficient of kinetic friction.

Graph between applied force and force of friction:

Contact Force:

$\mathrm{F}_{\mathrm{C}}=\sqrt{\mathrm{f}^2+\mathrm{N}^2}$

2.Angle of Friction ($\lambda$):The  angle which the resultant of the force of limiting friction fL and normal reaction N makes with the direction of normal reaction N.

$\tan \lambda=\mu_{\mathrm{s}}$

Angle of Repose :It is defined as the minimum angle of inclination of a plane with the horizontal at which a body placed on it just begins to slide down or equivalently the maximum angle of inclination of plane with the horizontal at which a body placed on it does not slide.

$\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{L}}=\mathrm{mg} \sin \theta ........(i)$

$\mathrm{~N}=\mathrm{mg} \cos \theta \\$

$\mathrm{~f}_{\mathrm{L}}=\mu \mathrm{N}=\mu \mathrm{mg} \cos \theta ........(ii)$

From (i) and (ii)

$\mu_s=\dfrac{\mathrm{f}_{\mathrm{L}}}{\mathrm{~N}}=\dfrac{\mathrm{mg} \sin \theta}{\mathrm{mg} \cos \theta}=\tan \theta \Rightarrow \theta=\tan ^{-1} \mu_s$

$\text { Angle of repose }(\theta)=\text { Angle of friction }(\lambda)$

Downward sliding on rough incline plane: If angle of inclination is greater than the angle of repose, then the body accelerates down the incline.

$\mathrm{a}=\mathrm{g}\left[\sin \theta-\mu_{\mathrm{k}} \cos \theta\right] \quad \text { hence } \mathrm{a}<\mathrm{g}$

For sliding down with constant velocity: a = 0

$\mathrm{g} \sin \theta=\mu_{\mathrm{k}} \mathrm{~g} \cos \theta$

$\tan \theta=\mu_{\mathrm{k}}$

Upward sliding on rough incline:

$a=g \sin \theta+\mu_k g \cos \theta$
